matching.reasoningTemplate: Tachypnoea with a mixed respiratory alkalosis/metabolic acidosis and tinnitus suggests salicylate poisoning.

clinicalPearls: Classic course: early nausea/vomiting and hyperventilation with respiratory alkalosis and alkaline urine, evolving to a mixed respiratory alkalosis plus high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis with paradoxical aciduria; late stages show acidemia with CNS and respiratory depression (p.3714).
Salicylates are the most common cause of drug-induced respiratory alkalosis, acting by direct stimulation of the medullary respiratory chemoreceptor (p.376).
Only part of the elevated anion gap is attributable to salicylate itself; concurrent lactic acid production and other endogenous unmeasured anions also contribute (p.370, p.3714).
Cerebral and pulmonary edema can develop in severe poisoning; non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema (ARDS) is a recognized complication (p.3705, p.3714).
Hypoglycemia, hypocalcemia, hypokalemia, and seizures can occur in salicylate toxicity (p.3714).
Ketosis can accompany salicylate poisoning and may mimic other causes of ketoacidosis (p.3705).
Salicylate is detected on quantitative serum assay; serum levels guide management and are usually available within an hour (p.3706).

Enteric-coated and sustained-release salicylate preparations cause delayed/slow absorption and can form gastric concretions (bezoars), acting as a 'toxic time-bomb' with continued rising levels (p.3705, p.3752).
harrison.pathophysiology: Salicylate increases sensitivity of the CNS respiratory center and directly stimulates the medullary chemoreceptor, driving hyperventilation and respiratory alkalosis. It also uncouples oxidative phosphorylation, inhibits Krebs cycle enzymes, and stimulates carbohydrate and lipid metabolism, generating unmeasured endogenous anions (and increased lactate) that produce a high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis (p.376, p.3714).
nonInfectiousMimics: Other high-anion-gap metabolic acidoses: methanol, ethylene glycol, alcoholic/diabetic/starvation ketoacidosis, lactic acidosis, kidney failure (p.412)
Other causes of ketosis: acetone, isopropyl alcohol, alcoholic ketoacidosis (p.3705)
Other causes of drug-induced respiratory alkalosis: theophylline/aminophylline; also sepsis, hepatic failure, pregnancy/progesterone (p.376)
additionalInvestigations: Serial quantitative serum salicylate level (guides management) (p.3706)
Anion gap and serum lactate (lactate typically lower than the anion gap in salicylate vs near-equal in shock/organ failure) (p.3705)
Serum glucose and calcium (risk of hypoglycemia, hypocalcemia) (p.3714)
Abdominal x-ray/CT may show radiopaque enteric-coated salicylate tablets or concretions (p.3706)
redFlags: Progressive acid-base disturbance / late acidemia with CNS and respiratory depression (p.3714)
Salicylate level >7 mmol/L (100 mg/dL) after acute overdose (p.3714)
pitfalls: Vigorous gastric lavage, if used, should be with isotonic saline, NOT NaHCO3 (p.370).
Only a portion of the anion gap is due to salicylate itself; do not assume the whole gap reflects drug level (p.370).
Acid (acidic) diuresis is never indicated and is potentially harmful (p.3752).
Acetazolamide can cause systemic metabolic acidosis if excreted bicarbonate is not replaced, which markedly reduces salicylate clearance (p.370).
Delayed/slow absorption from enteric-coated, sustained-release, or concretion-forming salicylate means a single early level can underestimate toxicity; repeat levels (p.3705, p.3752).
harrison.severityClassification: Stages by clinical/acid-base course: (1) early respiratory alkalosis with alkalemia, alkaluria, nausea/vomiting and hyperventilation; (2) mixed respiratory alkalosis plus high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis with paradoxical aciduria; (3) late acidemia with CNS and respiratory depression, cerebral and pulmonary edema in severe cases. Severe-toxicity markers include coma, cerebral edema, seizures, pulmonary edema, renal failure, progressive acid-base disturbance, and salicylate level >7 mmol/L (100 mg/dL) after acute overdose (p.3714).
